analogy.p: Imagine a row of people passing a bucket of water hand to hand (energy passing between particles). In a metal, there are also runners (delocalised electrons) who dash along the row carrying buckets quickly, so the transfer is rapid. In an insulator the people stand far apart or have no runners, so the buckets move slowly. A thicker wall is a longer row, so it takes longer. The analogy breaks down because particles do not pass a physical bucket; they transfer kinetic energy through collisions and vibrations.

bullets: Unwanted transfers are mostly to the **thermal store of the surroundings**, by friction, electrical resistance, air resistance, sound and heat loss.
**Lubrication** reduces friction between moving parts, so less kinetic energy is transferred as thermal energy.
**Thermal insulation** reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating, e.g. from a warm house to the cold outdoors.
Reducing wasted energy **increases efficiency** (useful output ÷ total input).
Streamlining reduces air resistance; low-resistance wires reduce heating in cables; both are further examples.
The wasted energy is **dissipated**, not destroyed; the aim is to stop it dissipating in the first place.
core.p: In almost every device or building some energy is transferred to places where it is not wanted, almost always as **thermal energy** spreading to the surroundings. Reducing these **unwanted energy transfers** makes devices more efficient and saves money and fuel. The specification asks you to **explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfers**, for example **lubrication** (to reduce friction) and **thermal insulation** (to reduce heat loss). The key idea is that you cannot stop energy being conserved, but you can reduce the amount that is wasted.

bullets: Friction: a force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact; it transfers kinetic energy to **thermal energy**.
A **lubricant** (oil, grease, graphite or a layer of air) **separates the surfaces** and lets them slide more easily.
Examples: oil in a car engine, grease on bicycle chains and wheel bearings, oil in door hinges.
Less friction means **less energy dissipated as heat** and **more of the input energy is usefully transferred**.
Lubrication also **reduces wear and overheating**, so parts last longer.
Friction is not always unwanted: brakes and shoe soles rely on it, so lubrication is only used where friction is a problem.
core.p: When two solid surfaces slide over each other, the tiny bumps on the surfaces catch and the **force of friction** acts against the motion. Work is done against friction, which transfers **kinetic energy to the thermal store** of the surfaces, making them hotter and wasting energy. A **lubricant** such as oil or grease forms a thin layer between the surfaces, so they slide past the lubricant instead of rubbing directly against each other. This lowers friction, reduces the thermal energy produced and also reduces wear.

bullets: **High** thermal conductivity = energy transferred **quickly** (good conductor), e.g. copper, aluminium, steel.
**Low** thermal conductivity = energy transferred **slowly** (good insulator), e.g. wool, polystyrene foam, fibreglass, air.
Thermal conductivity is a **property of the material**; thickness and area are separate factors.
Saucepans are made of metal (high conductivity) with plastic handles (low conductivity) so that the handle stays cool.
The **rate of energy transfer** is the energy transferred per second (a power, in watts).
A temperature difference is needed: energy is transferred from the **hotter** region to the **cooler** region.
core.p: **Thermal conductivity** tells you how well a material transfers energy by **conduction**. The **higher the thermal conductivity** of a material, the **higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction** across the material. Metals have high thermal conductivity, so energy flows through them quickly. Materials such as wool, foam and air have low thermal conductivity and are called **thermal insulators**: energy flows through them slowly. This property is a characteristic of the material and does not depend on its thickness.

bullets: In **all solids**, energy is passed from particle to particle by **vibrations/collisions** between neighbouring particles.
In **metals**, **delocalised electrons** carry energy quickly through the structure: this is why metals have high thermal conductivity.
In **gases**, particles are far apart and collide rarely, so conduction is very **slow**: this is why air is a good insulator.
**Liquids** have particles closer than gases, but conduction is still much less than in metals.
Trapping air in small pockets (foam, wool, feathers, double glazing) stops **convection** as well as limiting conduction.
Energy transfer by conduction continues until all parts reach the **same temperature**.
core.p: In a **solid**, particles are held in fixed positions and vibrate. When one end of a solid is heated, the particles there vibrate more strongly (they gain kinetic energy) and pass this energy on to neighbouring particles by **collisions** or through the bonds between them. In **metals** there are also **delocalised (free) electrons** that move through the structure, gaining kinetic energy when they are heated and transferring it quickly by colliding with ions and other electrons. This makes metals much better conductors than non-metals.

bullets: **Thicker walls** = **lower** rate of energy transfer by conduction (energy has further to travel).
**Lower thermal conductivity** walls = **lower** rate of energy transfer.
Therefore the building cools **more slowly** if it has thick walls of low thermal conductivity material.
The rate of cooling is also larger when the **temperature difference** between inside and outside is larger.
A bigger **surface area** also increases the rate of energy loss (more area for energy to escape).
Always mention both **thickness** and **thermal conductivity** when answering these questions.
core.h: Rate of energy transfer and the thickness of walls
core.p: The specification states that the **rate of cooling of a building depends on the thickness and thermal conductivity of its walls**. A thicker wall gives the energy a longer path to travel, so the rate of energy transfer is lower. A wall made from a material with lower thermal conductivity also transfers energy more slowly. So to keep a building warm, you use thick walls of low-conductivity materials. Both factors combine, and the greatest saving comes from the walls, roof and windows of the building that have the largest losses.

bullets: **Loft insulation** (fibreglass wool laid in the roof space): the trapped air in the fibres is a poor conductor and prevents convection, so less energy escapes through the roof.
**Cavity wall insulation**: foam injected into the gap between the two brick layers fills the air gap with small pockets of trapped air, so **convection** in the gap is stopped and conduction is low.
**Double glazing**: two panes of glass with an air gap (or vacuum/gas) between them; the gap has low thermal conductivity, so conduction through the window is reduced.
**Draught excluders** and sealed doors stop warm air escaping, reducing **convection** losses.
**Thick curtains** and carpets trap air and reduce energy transfer.
Most of the energy lost from an uninsulated house goes through the **roof and walls**.
core.p: A typical house loses energy through the roof, walls, windows, doors and floor. Each type of insulation targets one route for energy transfer. They all work by using materials with **low thermal conductivity**, often by trapping **air**, which is a poor conductor and cannot move to carry energy by convection when trapped in tiny pockets. Understanding how each method works lets you give explained answers, rather than just listing the method.

bullets: **Vacuum** between the two glass walls: there are no particles, so **no conduction and no convection** across the gap.
**Silvered (shiny) surfaces**: reflect **infrared radiation** back, reducing energy transfer by radiation.
**Plastic stopper**: a poor conductor, which reduces conduction through the top and stops convection currents escaping.
Glass is a poor conductor, so conduction through the walls of the flask is slow.
Small energy losses still occur through the neck and stopper, so the contents cool very slowly rather than not at all.
**Radiation** can travel through a vacuum, which is why reflective surfaces are needed.
core.p: A vacuum flask is designed to keep hot liquids hot (and cold liquids cold) by reducing energy transfer by **conduction, convection and radiation**. It has a double-walled container with a vacuum between the walls and silvered surfaces, and a stopper made of an insulator. Each feature targets a different transfer, which is exactly how it is asked in exam questions.

bullets: **Step 1**: use a beaker (or can) of the same size, placed inside a larger beaker with a gap that you fill with the insulating material being tested.
**Step 2**: heat water in a kettle, measure out the same volume (e.g. 100 cm³) using a **measuring cylinder** and pour it into the inner container at the same starting temperature (e.g. 80 °C).
**Step 3**: put on a **lid** (with a hole for a thermometer or temperature probe), start the stopwatch and record the temperature every minute for 10 minutes.
**Step 4**: repeat for each material, and also with **no insulation** as a control.
**Step 5**: repeat each test at least three times and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability.
**Step 6**: plot temperature against time and compare the temperature drops, or the gradients of the cooling curves.
core.p: A common practical investigates how effective different materials are as thermal insulators, by seeing how quickly hot water cools in a container surrounded by each material. The independent variable is the **insulating material** (or its thickness), the dependent variable is the **temperature fall** (or rate of cooling), and everything else must be **controlled** so that the test is fair. The best insulator is the material that gives the **smallest temperature drop** or the **lowest rate of cooling** in the same time.

bullets: **Independent variable**: type of insulating material (or thickness of the material).
**Dependent variable**: the temperature of the water after a set time, or the temperature fall (°C), or the rate of cooling (°C/min).
**Control variables**: starting temperature and volume of water, same container and lid, same thickness/mass of insulation, same time interval, same room temperature, no draughts.
**Measuring instruments**: thermometer or temperature probe (°C), stopwatch (s), measuring cylinder (cm³).
Using a **data logger and temperature probe** gives more precise, more frequent readings and removes reading errors.
The **no-insulation test** acts as a control to show how much each material reduces the cooling.
core.p: A valid investigation changes only one variable at a time. Since many things affect how fast water cools, you must keep all the others the same. Examiners often ask for **control variables**, and answers must be specific, for example 'the same starting temperature of the water', not just 'the same temperature'. You should also name the instrument used to measure each variable and its resolution.

bullets: **Hazard**: hot water or steam can scald; control by wearing eye protection, carrying the kettle carefully, standing up to work, and mopping spills straight away.
Use a **lid** and ensure the thermometer does not touch the base of the beaker so the reading is accurate.
**Source of error**: energy escapes through the lid and from the top of the water, which are not insulated; use a well-fitting insulating lid.
Reading a thermometer to the nearest 1 °C gives a **resolution** problem; use a digital probe (0.1 °C).
The water cools faster when much hotter than the room, so **start every test at the same temperature**.
To make results more **reliable**, repeat tests and calculate a mean; to be more **valid**, control all variables.
core.h: Risks, errors and improving the method
core.p: The main hazard is the **hot water**, which can scald. You should always describe a risk and how to control it, not just name it. Evaluating the method means recognising where energy might still be lost, which makes the results less accurate, and suggesting realistic improvements. Marks are available for identifying sources of error and explaining how a change improves the result.

bullets: The **gradient** of the graph at any point = rate of cooling = change in temperature ÷ change in time (°C/min).
The curve **flattens** as the water approaches the room temperature, because the temperature difference becomes smaller.
The **best insulator** has the curve that is highest after the same time, i.e. the smallest temperature drop.
Compare materials by the **temperature drop in the same time**, or by calculating the mean rate of cooling.
To find the rate at a particular time, draw a **tangent** to the curve and calculate its gradient (Higher tier skill).
If a curve does not start at the same temperature as another, the comparison is not fair.
core.p: A graph of temperature against time for cooling water is a curve that slopes downwards and gets **gradually shallower**. The steepness (gradient) at any point is the **rate of cooling** in °C per minute. The curve is steepest at the start because the temperature difference between the water and the surroundings is greatest, so energy is lost fastest. A better insulator gives a curve that falls more slowly (a shallower curve), ending at a higher final temperature.

bullets: **Efficiency** = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer; reducing waste raises efficiency.
**Payback time** = cost of installing the insulation ÷ money saved per year; shorter payback means more cost-effective.
Loft insulation is usually cheap with a short payback time; double glazing is expensive with a long payback time.
Insulation reduces fuel use and therefore **carbon dioxide emissions** from burning fuels.
**Particle model**: conduction depends on particle vibrations and delocalised electrons in metals.
**Energy conservation**: the energy not transferred through the walls stays in the house, so the total energy is still conserved.
core.h: Links to efficiency, cost and other topics
core.p: Insulation and lubrication are two practical ways to **increase efficiency**: they reduce the wasted energy so a larger fraction of the energy input is usefully transferred. In real life you must weigh the **cost** of the insulation against the money it saves on bills over time, which is the idea of **payback time**. This links to energy resources, to the particle model of conduction and to the idea that energy is conserved but dissipated.

bullets: **Mean rate of cooling = temperature fall ÷ time** (°C/min); for the example: none 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5, A 18 ÷ 10 = 1.8, B 10 ÷ 10 = 1.0 °C/min.
The **smallest** rate (or the **smallest fall**) means the **best insulator**: material B.
Compare only tests that start at the **same temperature** with the same volume of water and the same time.
Convert units if needed: 600 s = 10 min, so a fall of 10 °C in 600 s is 10 ÷ 600 = 0.017 °C/s.
The **rate at one moment** is the gradient of a tangent drawn on the curve (a Higher-tier skill).
A **percentage reduction** compares fairly: for B, (25 − 10) ÷ 25 × 100 = 60% less temperature fall than no insulation.
Always state a **conclusion** that uses the data: which material, which numbers, and why.
core.h: Calculating and comparing rates of cooling
core.p: To compare insulators fairly you turn the readings into a rate. The mean rate of cooling is the temperature fall divided by the time taken, in degrees Celsius per minute, and the material with the smallest rate is the best insulator. Because every test starts at the same temperature and runs for the same time, comparing the final temperatures gives the same ranking, which is a quicker check. You should also be able to read a cooling curve: a steeper part means faster cooling and the curve levels off as the water approaches room temperature.

exam: **Explain how loft insulation reduces heat loss (2 marks)**: 'trapped air / fibres have low thermal conductivity so rate of energy transfer by conduction is reduced; air cannot circulate so convection is reduced'.
**Thickness and conductivity (2 marks)**: say both 'the thicker the wall the lower the rate of energy transfer' and 'lower thermal conductivity gives lower rate'.
**Lubrication (2 marks)**: 'oil reduces friction between the moving parts, so less energy is transferred to the thermal store / less energy is wasted'.

**Describe the investigation (4 to 6 marks)**: same volume and starting temperature of water, measure the temperature at regular intervals, repeat with each material, repeat for a mean, say which variable is changed and measured.
**Control variables**: give specific ones (volume, starting temperature, container, thickness of insulation, time interval, lid).
**Risks**: hot water scalds; control with eye protection and care pouring, mop spills immediately.
**Graphs**: label axes with quantity and unit; join points with a smooth curve; find rate of cooling from the gradient or tangent.
**Evaluate (3 to 6 marks)**: weigh up cost, payback time, effectiveness and environmental benefit and give a justified conclusion.
**Use key phrases**: 'low thermal conductivity', 'rate of energy transfer', 'dissipated to the surroundings', 'trapped air'.
**Compare materials**: use data, e.g. 'material B fell by only 10 °C compared with 25 °C with no insulation, so it is the better insulator'.
**Required practical conclusion (3 marks):** quote the temperature falls or mean rates for each material, name the best insulator, and link it to its lower thermal conductivity.

mistakes.r: Insulation reduces the rate at which energy is transferred from the warm inside to the cold outside.
Warm air rises (convection); loft insulation traps air and has low thermal conductivity, so less energy is conducted through the roof.
mistakes.w: Heat rises, so loft insulation stops heat rising.

mistakes.r: A thicker wall reduces the rate of energy transfer; energy still passes through more slowly.
mistakes.w: Thicker wall means energy cannot get through.

mistakes.r: Metals have delocalised electrons that transfer energy quickly, giving a high thermal conductivity.
mistakes.w: Metals are good conductors because they are hot/shiny.

mistakes.r: Say the same starting temperature and the same volume of water in the same container.
mistakes.w: The same temperature of water (as a control variable).

mistakes.r: Wool traps air, a poor conductor, which reduces the rate of energy transfer from the body.
The vacuum stops conduction and convection; silvered surfaces reduce radiation.
mistakes.w: A vacuum flask works because a vacuum stops all heat.

mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction by separating surfaces, so less kinetic energy is transferred to thermal energy.
Insulation only reduces the rate of energy transfer; the house still cools, but more slowly.
mistakes.w: Saying that insulation stops energy leaving a house completely.

mistakes.r: Rate of transfer depends on both thickness and thermal conductivity of the material.
mistakes.w: Saying thicker walls always give lower energy loss whatever they are made of.

summary: You must be able to explain how unwanted energy transfers can be reduced, mainly by lubrication and thermal insulation, and know that a higher thermal conductivity means a higher rate of energy transfer by conduction, and that a building cools more slowly if its walls are thicker and made of a low thermal conductivity material. You also need to describe and evaluate an investigation into how well different materials insulate. This matters because it links energy conservation to efficiency, cost and everyday design.

worked.ans: Material B is the best insulator; its mean rate of cooling is 1.0 °C/min (compared with 2.5 °C/min with no insulation and 1.8 °C/min for A).
worked.q: In a test, 100 cm³ of water at 80 °C was cooled for 10 minutes with different insulation. Final temperatures: no insulation 55 °C, material A 62 °C, material B 70 °C. Which is the best insulator? Calculate the mean rate of cooling for material B. (4 marks)
steps: The smallest temperature fall is for material B, so B is the best insulator.
Mean rate of cooling for B = temperature fall ÷ time = 10 ÷ 10 = 1.0 °C/min.

worked.ans: Cavity wall foam traps air in tiny pockets; air is a poor conductor so the rate of energy transfer by conduction is low, and the air cannot move, so there are no convection currents; therefore less energy is transferred from inside the house to the outside.
worked.q: Explain how cavity wall insulation reduces the energy lost from a house. (3 marks)
steps: The foam fills the air gap between the walls.
It contains many small pockets of trapped air, which has a low thermal conductivity.
The trapped air cannot circulate, so convection currents in the cavity are stopped.
